references.text: Proverbs encourages guarding the heart above all, for life flows from it—parallel to the idea that what is in the heart comes out through the mouth.
The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life—emphasizing the connection between a good heart and good speech.
Thoughtless words can wound like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing—showing the contrast between good and evil speech as fruit of the heart's condition.
The lips of the wise spread knowledge, but the mouth of fools pours out folly—parallel to the principle that the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart.
The righteous heart considers how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil—closely tied to Jesus' words that the heart determines what the mouth speaks.

Matthew's parallel passage where Jesus says the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart, and that a good person brings forth good from their good treasure, while an evil person brings forth evil from their evil treasure.
Jesus says that what comes out of the mouth originates in the heart, and this makes a person unclean—expanding on the connection between heart and speech.

James writes that from the same mouth come blessing and cursing, using the image of a spring that cannot give both fresh and salt water—emphasizing that the condition of the heart is revealed in speech.
The wise heart makes his mouth prudent and adds learning to his lips—showing a direct link between the wisdom of the heart and the quality of speech.
The immediate context where Jesus speaks about how a good tree does not bear bad fruit—the heart as a treasure chest is an elaboration on the fruit metaphor.
